components.note: 亻 (person) — 伯 names a male relative, a person in the family.
白 (bái) gives the sound — close to bó, sharing the same initial and a similar rhyme.

example.hanzi: 我爸爸的哥哥是我的伯伯。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bàba de gēge shì wǒ de bóbo.
example.english: My dad's older brother is my uncle.
example.fact: Chinese has no single word for 'uncle' — 伯伯 specifically means an older paternal uncle, showing how Mandarin kinship terms encode age and family side.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 慢 describes an unhurried state of mind or pace.
曼 (màn) gives the sound — an exact match with 慢.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī wūguī zǒu de hěn màn.
example.english: This turtle walks very slowly.
example.fact: Tortoises and turtles are famous around the world for being among the slowest-moving animals.

meanings: Europe (abbr. for 歐洲|欧洲[Ou1 zhou1])
European Union (abbr. for 歐盟|欧盟[Ou1 meng2])

example.english: Europe has many countries.
example.fact: Europe is made up of dozens of countries, each with its own language and culture.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 换 describes an action done by hand, such as swapping or exchanging.
奂 (huàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 换.

example.english: Please help me exchange money.
example.fact: 换 is the everyday word travelers use for exchanging currency, as in 换钱 (huàn qián), when arriving in a new country.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — 闻 originally meant 'to hear,' later extending to 'smell' and 'news.'
门 (mén) contributes the rhyme -en, close to wén's sound, though the initial has since shifted.

example.english: I watch the news every day.
example.fact: 闻 originally meant 'to hear' — 新闻 (xīnwén, 'news') literally means 'newly heard things.'

etymologyHint: A person 㔾 at the edge of a cliff 厃; 厃 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 厃 depicts a steep, overhanging cliff edge.
㔾 depicts a person crouching — together with 厃, the image of someone perched at a cliff's edge gave 危 its meaning 'dangerous.'

example.pinyin: Shān shàng de lù hěn wēixiǎn.
example.english: The mountain road is very dangerous.
example.fact: Mount Everest, the world's tallest mountain, is famous for the dangerous conditions climbers face near its summit.

etymologyHint: A heart 忄 faced with death 亡; 亡 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 忙 describes an inner state, here one of pressure or urgency.
亡 depicts loss or fleeing — paired with the heart, it suggests a mind under pressure, giving 忙 its meaning 'busy, rushed.'

example.english: Mom is busy every day.
example.fact: 忙 is often doubled into 帮忙 (bāngmáng, 'to help'), literally meaning to lend a hand to someone's busyness.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — 核 originally named the hard pit inside a fruit.
亥 (hài) gives an approximate sound, close to hé though the vowel has since shifted.

example.english: A peach's pit is very hard.
example.fact: 核's meaning expanded from a fruit's pit to 'core' or 'nucleus' generally, as in 核能 (hénéng, 'nuclear energy').

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暗 describes the absence of light, the opposite of a bright sun.
音 (yīn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading àn has diverged.

example.english: It's very dark at night.
example.fact: 暗 appears in 暗恋 (ànliàn), meaning 'secret love' — literally a 'hidden, dark' romantic feeling, a common word in Chinese dramas.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姐 names a female relative, an older sister.
且 (qiě) gives the rhyme, close to jiě though the tone differs.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiějie bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
example.english: My older sister is three years older than me.
example.fact: Mandarin has no single word for 'sister' — 姐姐 (jiějie) means specifically 'older sister,' while 妹妹 (mèimei) means 'younger sister.'

etymologyHint: A border 八 dividing people 人

components.note: 人 (person) forms the top of the character.
八, shown here as a dividing line, suggests separation or a boundary — together with 人 above, giving 介 its meaning 'to lie between, to introduce.'

example.hanzi: 让我介绍一下我的朋友。
example.pinyin: Ràng wǒ jièshào yíxià wǒ de péngyou.
example.english: Let me introduce my friend.
example.fact: 介绍 (jièshào, 'to introduce') is one of the first practical phrases Mandarin learners use when meeting someone new.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坏 relates to something crumbling or deteriorating, like broken soil.
不 (bù) reflects an old phonetic link that has largely faded in the modern pronunciation huài.

example.english: This apple has gone bad.
example.fact: 坏 is commonly paired with 了 to describe something that has just broken or spoiled — one of the first adjective-plus-了 patterns beginners learn.

etymologyHint: To ask 讠 for something 寸

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 讨 involves speaking, as in asking or discussing.
寸 (a hand/small measure) — combined with speech, suggests reaching out verbally to ask for something, giving 讨 its meaning 'to ask for, to discuss.'

example.english: We are discussing homework.
example.fact: 讨论 (tǎolùn, 'to discuss') pairs 讨 ('to seek out') with 论 ('to talk over') — a common classroom word.

meanings: used in place names, notably 高麗|高丽[Gao1 li2] and 麗水|丽水[Li2 shui3]
etymologyHint: Simplified form of 麗; the antlers of a deer 鹿

components.note: 丽 is the simplified form of 麗, which depicted the ornate antlers of a deer (鹿) — a fitting image behind its meaning 'beautiful, magnificent.'

example.english: Guilin's scenery is very beautiful.
example.fact: Guilin, in southern China, is famous worldwide for the beautiful karst mountain landscapes along its Li River.

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè shànliáng de rén.
example.english: He is a kind person.
example.fact: 良 appears in words like 良好 (liánghǎo, 'good') and 善良 (shànliáng, 'kind-hearted'), always carrying a positive, virtuous sense.

components.note: 广 (a wide building) — 序 relates to arrangement, as in the ordered layout of a hall.
予 (yǔ) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though it has diverged from the modern reading xù.

example.english: Please line up in order.
example.fact: 序 combines with 顺 to form 顺序 (shùnxù, 'order, sequence'), a common word for describing how things are arranged.

example.english: The sun rises from the east every day.
example.fact: The sun always rises in the east because of the direction Earth rotates.

example.english: That person is in prison.
example.fact: 监 combines with 狱 to form 监狱 (jiānyù, 'prison'), and on its own also means 'to supervise, to oversee.'

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè línshí de bànfǎ.
example.english: This is a temporary solution.
example.fact: 临时 (línshí, 'temporary') is one of the most common uses of 临 in daily Mandarin, as in 临时工 (línshígōng, 'temp worker').

components.note: 亮 is traditionally read as a picture of a lit oil lamp raised on a stand, radiating light — a fitting image for its meaning 'bright, radiant.'

example.english: The moon is very bright tonight.
example.fact: The full moon is the brightest object in the night sky besides artificial lights, because it reflects sunlight toward Earth.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 露 names a form of moisture related to weather.
路 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 露.

example.english: There is dew on the grass in the morning.
example.fact: Dew forms when moist night air cools and condenses on cool surfaces like grass, a common weather phenomenon worldwide.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒngyuǎn ài wǒ de jiārén.
example.english: I will always love my family.
example.fact: 永 almost always appears paired with 远 to form 永远 (yǒngyuǎn, 'forever'), rarely standing alone in modern Mandarin.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呼 describes an action of the mouth, such as calling out or breathing.
乎 (hū) gives the sound — an exact match with 呼.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiǎnchá le tā de hūxī.
example.english: The doctor checked his breathing.
example.fact: 呼吸 (hūxī, 'to breathe') combines 呼 ('to exhale') and 吸 ('to inhale') — the two opposite halves of breathing joined into one word.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 味 relates to taste, sensed in the mouth.
未 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 味.

example.pinyin: Zhège tāng de wèidao hěn hǎo.
example.english: This soup tastes very good.
example.fact: 味道 (wèidao) means both 'taste, flavor' and more broadly 'feeling,' showing how 味 extends from physical taste to sensory experience in general.

components.note: 里 (village, a unit of land) — 野 describes open country beyond the village.
予 (yǔ) reflects an older phonetic link, though the modern readings yě and yǔ have since diverged.

example.hanzi: 森林里有很多野生动物。
example.pinyin: Sēnlín lǐ yǒu hěn duō yěshēng dòngwù.
example.english: There are many wild animals in the forest.
example.fact: Forests are home to a huge share of the world's wild animal species, more than almost any other habitat.

components.note: 木 (wood) — racks and frames like 架 were traditionally built of wood.
加 (jiā) gives a rhyme close to jià, with the tone shifted.

example.pinyin: Shūjià shàng yǒu hěn duō shū.
example.english: There are many books on the bookshelf.
example.fact: 架 as a noun means 'rack, frame' (as in 书架, 'bookshelf'), while as a verb it can mean 'to fight' (打架, 'to quarrel') — quite different senses for one character.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 域 names a bounded area of land, a territory.
或 (huò) reflects the character's historical phonetic root; the modern reading yù has since diverged.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè ānjìng de qūyù.
example.english: This is a quiet area.
example.fact: 域 commonly appears in words like 区域 (qūyù, 'region') and 领域 (lǐngyù, 'field/domain'), always carrying the sense of a bounded territory.

components.note: 氵 (water) — sand forms as water erodes rock over time.
少 (shǎo) shares the initial sh- with shā, though the vowel has since shifted.

example.english: There is almost no water in the desert.
example.fact: The Sahara, in North Africa, is one of the largest hot deserts in the world.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掉 relates to dropping something from the hand.
卓 (zhuó) reflects an older phonetic connection that has faded in the modern pronunciation diào.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī diào dào dìshang le.
example.english: My phone fell on the ground.
example.fact: 掉 is often used after other verbs to mean 'away, off,' as in 扔掉 (rēngdiào, 'to throw away') or 忘掉 (wàngdiào, 'to forget').

meanings: (bound form) to tie up; to tighten up

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 括 describes gathering or bundling things together by hand.
舌 (shé) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern pronunciation kuò has diverged considerably.

example.english: The price includes breakfast.
example.fact: 括 almost always appears in words like 包括 (bāokuò, 'to include') or 括号 (kuòhào, 'parentheses'), rarely standing alone in modern Mandarin.

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 舰 names a large military ship.
见 (jiàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 舰.

example.english: The warship sails on the sea.
example.fact: 舰 always refers to a large military ship, as in 军舰 (jūnjiàn, 'warship') or 航空母舰 (hángmǔjiàn, 'aircraft carrier').

meanings: used in the names of various aquatic animals that are not fish (including abalone 鮑魚|鲍鱼[bao4 yu2], alligators and crocodiles 鱷魚|鳄鱼[e4 yu2] and octopi 章魚|章鱼[zhang1 yu2])

components.note: 鱼 is a simplified picture of a fish — the top traces its head and fins, and the strokes below represent its body and tail.

example.english: Chinese people like to eat fish for the New Year.
example.fact: 鱼 (yú, 'fish') sounds like 余 (yú, 'surplus'), so eating fish at Chinese New Year is a tradition symbolizing abundance for the year ahead.

example.pinyin: Zhège shāngdiàn mài hěn duō zázhì.
example.english: This store sells many magazines.
example.fact: 杂 means 'mixed, miscellaneous' and appears in 杂志 (zázhì, 'magazine') — literally a mix of many topics — and 复杂 (fùzá, 'complicated').

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 误 began as a mistake in speech, later broadening to 'error' in general.
吴 (wú) gives a sound close to wù, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 对不起，我犯了一个错误。
example.pinyin: Duìbuqǐ, wǒ fàn le yí gè cuòwù.
example.english: Sorry, I made a mistake.
example.fact: 错误 (cuòwù, 'mistake') combines two near-synonyms, 错 and 误, both meaning 'wrong' — a common way Mandarin pairs related characters into one word.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 湾 names a curved body of water, a bay.
弯 (wān) gives the sound — an exact match with 湾.

example.english: Taiwan is an island.
example.fact: Taiwan is an island located off the southeastern coast of mainland China.

meanings: short name for Jilin 吉林[Ji2 lin2]
etymologyHint: The words 口 of a scholar 士

components.note: 士 depicts a scholar or gentleman.
口 (mouth) — the words of a wise, respected person were seen as auspicious, giving 吉 its meaning 'lucky, good.'

example.hanzi: 数字八在中国是吉利的数字。
example.pinyin: Shùzì bā zài Zhōngguó shì jílì de shùzì.
example.english: The number eight is a lucky number in China.
example.fact: In Chinese culture, the number eight (八) is considered lucky because it sounds similar to 发 (fā), which relates to wealth and prosperity.

components.note: 冫 (ice) — melting ice shrinks away, an image linked to 减's meaning 'to decrease.'
咸 (xián) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading jiǎn has diverged.

example.english: Ten minus five equals five.
example.fact: 减 is the standard Mandarin word for subtraction, used in basic math the same way 加 (jiā) is used for addition.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 编 originally described weaving or knitting threads together.
扁 (biǎn) gives a sound close to biān, with the tone shifted.

example.pinyin: Tā zài biān yí jiàn máoyī.
example.english: She is knitting a sweater.
example.fact: 编 originally meant weaving bamboo strips into books, before paper existed, which is why it also means 'to compile, to edit,' as in 编辑 (biānjí, 'editor').

meanings: abbr. for Hubei 湖北省[Hu2 bei3 Sheng3] and Hunan 湖南省[Hu2 nan2 Sheng3] provinces together
Chinese kingdom during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States Periods (722–221 BC)

example.english: He speaks very clearly.
example.fact: 楚 was also the name of a powerful ancient Chinese kingdom during the Warring States period, over two thousand years ago.

etymologyHint: To stop 止 flexing one's muscles ⺼

components.note: 止 depicts a foot coming to a stop.
⺼ (flesh, muscle) — pausing to make an effort willingly gave 肯 its meaning 'to be willing, to agree.'

example.english: He is willing to help friends.
example.fact: 肯 is most often used right before another verb to mean 'willing to,' as in 肯帮忙 (kěn bāngmáng, 'willing to help').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 测 originally referred to measuring the depth of water.
则 (zé) gives a rhyme close to cè, with the tone and initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 我们在测量教室的长度。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài cèliáng jiàoshì de chángdù.
example.english: We are measuring the length of the classroom.
example.fact: 测 originally meant measuring the depth of water, and later broadened to 'measure, survey' in general, as in 测量 (cèliáng).

components.note: 攵 (a striking hand) — 败 relates to being struck down or defeated.
贝 (bèi) gives a sound close to bài, sharing the same initial.

example.english: He failed the exam.
example.fact: 败 combines with 失 to form 失败 (shībài, 'to fail') and with 打 to form 打败 (dǎbài, 'to defeat'), both built around 败's core sense of 'loss, defeat.'

etymologyHint: To stop 至 under a roof 尸 (variant of 厂)

components.note: 尸, here a variant of 厂, depicts a roof or shelter.
至 depicts arriving or coming to rest — settling under a roof gave 屋 its meaning 'house, room.'

example.english: This room is very clean.
example.fact: 屋 usually refers to a single room or small building, while 房 (fáng) is the more general word for 'house' — the two often appear together as 房屋 (fángwū).

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跑 describes an action done with the feet, running.
包 (bāo) gives a sound close to pǎo, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: Cheetahs run very fast.
example.fact: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals in the world, able to reach speeds no other land animal can match.

etymologyHint: Two eyes shut 林 at night 夕

components.note: 林 here depicts eyes shut in sleep, not its usual meaning 'forest.'
夕 (evening, night) — sleeping at night is when dreams occur, giving 梦 its meaning 'dream.'

example.hanzi: 昨晚我做了一个奇怪的梦。
example.pinyin: Zuówǎn wǒ zuò le yí gè qíguài de mèng.
example.english: Last night I had a strange dream.
example.fact: People usually dream during a stage of sleep called REM sleep, though scientists still don't fully understand why we dream.

etymologyHint: A hand 攵 tossing seeds from a basket

components.note: 散 traditionally depicts a hand (攵) scattering something, like seeds tossed from a basket — the image behind its meaning 'to scatter, disperse.'

example.pinyin: Kāihuì hòu dàjiā jiù sàn le.
example.english: After the meeting, everyone dispersed.
example.fact: 散 appears in 散步 (sànbù, 'to take a walk') and 分散 (fēnsàn, 'to scatter'), always carrying a sense of spreading apart or loosening.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 温 originally described warm water.
昷 (wēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 温.

example.english: Today's temperature is very high.
example.fact: 温 combines with 度 to form 温度 (wēndù, 'temperature') and with 暖 to form 温暖 (wēnnuǎn, 'warm'), always carrying a mild, warm sense.

etymologyHint: A fence 囗 built around a tree 木

components.note: 囗 depicts an enclosure or fence.
木 (tree) — a tree hemmed in by a fence, unable to grow freely, gave 困 its meaning 'trapped, difficult.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān hěn kùn, xiǎng shuìjiào.
example.english: I'm very sleepy today, I want to sleep.
example.fact: Besides 'trapped, difficult,' 困 commonly means 'sleepy' in everyday speech, as in 我很困 ('I'm sleepy') — one character with two very different senses.

meanings: classifier for blows of a sword

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剑 names an edged weapon, a sword.
佥 (qiān) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though it has diverged from the modern reading jiàn.

example.english: That sword is very sharp.
example.fact: Swords like 剑 play a central role in Chinese martial arts and classic wuxia stories, often symbolizing a warrior's skill and honor.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渐 relates to a gradual flow, like water advancing bit by bit.
斩 (zhǎn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though it has diverged from the modern reading jiàn.

example.english: The weather is gradually getting cold.
example.fact: 渐 is almost always doubled as 渐渐 (jiànjiàn, 'gradually'), describing a slow, steady change over time.

etymologyHint: To seal 寸 something with a handful of mortar 土

components.note: 圭, made of two 土 (earth) stacked together, depicts a handful of mortar or soil.
寸 (a hand/small measure) — sealing something shut with packed mortar gave 封 its meaning 'to seal, to close.'

example.pinyin: Zhè fēng xìn shì gěi nǐ de.
example.english: This letter is for you.
example.fact: 封 is the measure word for letters in Mandarin (一封信, 'one letter'), tying back to its original meaning of a sealed package.

components.note: 攵 (a hand taking action) — 救 describes the act of rescuing someone.
求 (qiú) gives a sound close to jiù, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.pinyin: Xiāofángyuán jiù le nà zhī māo.
example.english: The firefighter saved that cat.
example.fact: 救 appears in 救命 (jiùmìng, 'help! / save my life'), one of the most important emergency phrases to know in Mandarin.

meanings: short name for Guizhou 貴州|贵州[Gui4 zhou1]

components.note: 贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) — 贵 relates to worth and cost.

example.english: This watch is very expensive.
example.fact: 贝 (shell) was ancient China's earliest form of currency, which is why so many money- and value-related characters, including 贵, contain 贝.

components.note: 木 (wood) — early spears and rifle stocks were made of wood.
仓 (cāng) gives a sound close to qiāng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: The police carry guns.
example.fact: 枪 originally meant 'spear,' a wooden weapon, and its meaning later extended to 'gun' once firearms were introduced.

components.note: 缶 (a clay jar) — 缺 relates to something broken or missing, like a cracked vessel.
夬 (guài) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading quē has diverged.

example.english: We're short one person.
example.fact: 缺 appears in 缺点 (quēdiǎn, 'shortcoming') and 缺少 (quēshǎo, 'to lack'), always carrying the sense of something missing or insufficient.

meanings: building of two or more stories

components.note: 木 (wood) — buildings were traditionally framed with wood.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 楼.

example.english: I live on the fifth floor.
example.fact: 楼 means both 'building' (of multiple stories) and 'floor, story' within one, so 五楼 can mean either 'Building 5' or 'the 5th floor,' depending on context.

example.pinyin: Zhège xiàn yǒu hěn duō xiǎo cūnzhuāng.
example.english: This county has many small villages.
example.fact: 县 (county) is one of the oldest administrative units in China, used for well over two thousand years to divide up the country's territory.

example.english: He is a Buddhist monk.
example.fact: 尚 appears in 和尚 (héshang, 'Buddhist monk') and also independently means 'still, yet' or 'to esteem,' as in 崇尚 (chóngshàng, 'to uphold').

components.note: 毛 (hair) — 毫 originally meant a fine, thin hair.

example.english: One millimeter is very short.
example.fact: 毫 originally meant 'fine hair,' an image of something extremely thin, which is why it's used in 毫米 (háomǐ, 'millimeter') and 毫升 (háoshēng, 'milliliter') for tiny units.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ zhuōzi yí dào nàbiān.
example.english: Please move the table over there.
example.fact: 移 combines with 动 to form 移动 (yídòng, 'to move'), a common word for changing position, including in 移动电话 (yídòng diànhuà, 'mobile phone').

components.note: 女 (woman) — 娘 names a female relative, mother or young woman.
良 (liáng) gives a sound close to niáng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: That girl is very pretty.
example.fact: 娘 appears in 姑娘 (gūniang, 'girl') and 新娘 (xīnniáng, 'bride'), and in some regions is also simply the word for 'mother.'

components.note: 月, appearing twice side by side, originally depicted two people (or two strings of shells) together — giving 朋 its meaning 'friend, companion.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zuì hǎo de péngyou.
example.english: He is my best friend.
example.fact: 朋友 (péngyou, 'friend') pairs two related characters, 朋 and 友, both meaning 'companion,' into one common word.

etymologyHint: A painting on an easel; compare 畫, which includes the brush

components.note: 画 depicts a picture set within a frame — the traditional form 畫 additionally showed a hand holding a brush above it.

example.english: This painting is very beautiful.
example.fact: 画 works as both a noun ('a painting,' as in 一幅画) and a verb ('to draw, to paint') without changing form.

etymologyHint: Cutting 刂 a piece of jade 王 in two, symbolizing two classes

components.note: 王 here is a variant of 玉 (jade), appearing once on each side of the character.
刂 (knife) — cutting a piece of jade in two, symbolizing a division into groups, gave 班 its meaning 'class, group.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen bān yǒu sānshí gè xuésheng.
example.english: Our class has thirty students.
example.fact: 班 is the standard word for a school 'class' or work 'shift,' as in 上班 (shàngbān, 'to go to work').

etymologyHint: Known 知 clearly 日; 知 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 知 (to know) forms the upper part of the character.
日 (sun, clarity) — knowledge seen as clearly as the sun gave 智 its meaning 'wisdom.'

example.english: He is very wise.
example.fact: In Western culture, the owl is traditionally a symbol of wisdom, an association going back to ancient Greek mythology and the goddess Athena.

etymologyHint: A man standing with arrows pointing to his armpits

components.note: 亦 originally depicted a standing figure with two marks pointing to the armpits; its literal meaning faded long ago, leaving only the abstract sense 'also, too.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan chá, yì xǐhuan kāfēi.
example.english: I like tea, and I also like coffee.
example.fact: 亦 is a literary equivalent of 也 ('also'), still used today in set phrases like 反之亦然 (fǎnzhī yìrán, 'vice versa').

components.note: 耳 is a simplified picture of the outer shape of a human ear.

example.english: A rabbit's ears are very long.
example.fact: Rabbits have unusually long ears, which help them hear predators from far away and also help release body heat.

meanings: (coll.) used like 嗯[en4] in online chat, expressing agreement

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恩 relates to feelings of gratitude and kindness.
因 (yīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 恩.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn gǎn'ēn nǐ de bāngzhù.
example.english: I'm very grateful for your help.
example.fact: 恩 appears in 感恩 (gǎn'ēn, 'to be grateful') and 恩人 (ēnrén, 'a person who helped you greatly'), always carrying a sense of kindness received.

components.note: 矢 (arrow) — arrows were historically used as a measuring standard, tied to 短's meaning 'short.'
豆 (dòu) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading duǎn has diverged.

example.english: Her hair is very short.
example.fact: 短 is the direct opposite of 长 (cháng, 'long'), and the two are often used together to ask about length, as in 长还是短? ('long or short?').

components.note: 手 (hand) — 掌 names the palm, part of the hand.
尚 (shàng) gives a rhyme close to zhǎng, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 他用手掌拍了一下桌子。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng shǒuzhǎng pāi le yíxià zhuōzi.
example.english: He slapped the table with his palm.
example.fact: 掌 also means 'to be in charge of,' as in 掌握 (zhǎngwò, 'to grasp, to master') — holding something firmly in one's palm extended to holding control over it.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恐 describes fear felt in the heart.
巩 (gǒng) gives a sound close to kǒng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.pinyin: Wǒ kǒngpà míngtiān yào xià yǔ.
example.english: I'm afraid it will rain tomorrow.
example.fact: 恐 combines with 龙 to form 恐龙 (kǒnglóng, 'dinosaur') — literally 'terror dragon,' matching the Greek-derived meaning of the English word.

etymologyHint: To leave 辶 something valuable 贵 behind

components.note: 辶 (to walk, to move) — suggests departing or leaving.
贵 (valuable, precious) — leaving something valuable behind gave 遗 its meaning 'to lose, to leave behind.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn yíhàn bù néng cānjiā.
example.english: I regret that I can't attend.
example.fact: 遗 combines with 憾 to form 遗憾 (yíhàn, 'regret, pity'), one of the most common ways to express disappointment politely in Mandarin.

components.note: 囗 (an enclosure) — something firmly closed in is secure, tied to 固's meaning 'solid, firm.'
古 (gǔ) gives a rhyme close to gù, with the tone shifted.

example.english: This bridge is very sturdy.
example.fact: 固 combines with 坚 to form 坚固 (jiāngù, 'sturdy, solid'), and appears alone in words like 固定 (gùdìng, 'fixed').

etymologyHint: A cloth 巾 or straw 艹 mat in the house 广

components.note: 广 depicts a simple roofed building or shelter.
巾 (cloth) — together with a grass-like element above it, suggests a woven straw or cloth mat inside the shelter, giving 席 its meaning 'mat, seat.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì xuéshēng huì de zhǔxí.
example.english: He is the chairman of the student council.
example.fact: 席 originally meant a woven mat used for sitting, which is why 主席 (zhǔxí, 'chairman') literally means 'main seat' — the seat of honor.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 松 names a type of tree, the pine.
公 (gōng) gives a rhyme close to sōng, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 松树在冬天也是绿色的。
example.pinyin: Sōngshù zài dōngtiān yě shì lǜsè de.
example.english: Pine trees are green even in winter.
example.fact: Pine trees are evergreens, meaning they keep their green needles all year round, even through winter.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — an older sense of 秘 was linked to grain kept out of sight, before it narrowed to 'secret.'
必 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 秘.

example.english: This is a secret.
example.fact: 秘 almost always appears in 秘密 (mìmì, 'secret') or 秘书 (mìshū, 'secretary,' originally 'keeper of secret documents').

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.

example.english: Thank you for the gift.
example.fact: 谢谢 (xièxie), doubling 谢, is one of the very first words most people learn in Mandarin — the standard way to say 'thank you.'

meanings: Lu, an ancient state of China 魯國|鲁国[Lu3 guo2]
etymologyHint: To talk 日 like a fish 鱼

components.note: 鱼 (fish) forms the top of the character.
日, placed beneath the fish, was linked to the idea of speaking crudely or bluntly, giving 鲁 its meaning 'rash, uncouth.'

example.hanzi: 鲁迅是著名的中国作家。
example.pinyin: Lǔ Xùn shì zhùmíng de Zhōngguó zuòjiā.
example.english: Lu Xun is a famous Chinese writer.
example.fact: Lu Xun is widely regarded as one of the most influential Chinese writers of the 20th century.

meanings: (bound form) to encounter; to happen upon; to meet unplanned

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — encountering someone often happens while moving or traveling.
禺 (yú) gives a sound close to yù, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 我在路上遇到了老朋友。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài lùshang yùdào le lǎo péngyou.
example.english: I ran into an old friend on the road.
example.fact: 遇 combines with 到 to form 遇到 (yùdào, 'to encounter, to run into'), describing an unplanned meeting or event.

etymologyHint: A home 广 with a servant 隶

components.note: 广 depicts a simple roofed building, a home.
隶 depicts a servant or laborer — a household with help was traditionally a sign of ease and well-being, giving 康 its meaning 'healthy, peaceful.'

example.english: Wishing you good health.
example.fact: 康 almost always appears with 健 in 健康 (jiànkāng, 'healthy'), one of the most common well-wishes in Mandarin.

etymologyHint: A tiger 虍 striking fear into the heart 心

components.note: 虍 depicts a tiger's head or stripes.
心 (heart) — a heart facing a tiger's threat gave 虑 its meaning 'to worry, to be concerned.'

example.english: We need to consider this problem.
example.fact: 虑 almost always appears in 考虑 (kǎolǜ, 'to consider') or 顾虑 (gùlǜ, 'worry, misgiving'), rarely standing alone.

etymologyHint: Two men, one alive 土 and one dead 干; the living one is lucky

components.note: The upper part, related to 土, traditionally depicted one person's fate.
干 depicted a contrasting fate — the character set two outcomes side by side, with the fortunate one giving 幸 its meaning 'lucky, fortunate.'

example.english: I'm very lucky to know you.
example.fact: 幸 combines with 运 to form 幸运 (xìngyùn, 'lucky') and with 福 to form 幸福 (xìngfú, 'happiness, blessed'), both very common words.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 均 relates to leveling land evenly.
匀 (yún) gives a rhyme close to jūn, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 这些苹果的大小很均匀。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē píngguǒ de dàxiǎo hěn jūnyún.
example.english: These apples are very even in size.
example.fact: 均 combines with 匀 to form 均匀 (jūnyún, 'even, uniform'), and alone can mean 'average,' as in 平均 (píngjūn, 'average').

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 销 originally meant to melt metal.
肖 (xiào) gives a rhyme close to xiāo, with the tone shifted.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā shāngdiàn zài cùxiāo shāngpǐn.
example.english: This store is having a sale.
example.fact: 销 originally meant 'to melt metal,' and later broadened to 'to sell' or 'to cancel,' as in 促销 (cùxiāo, 'to promote sales') and 取消 (qǔxiāo, 'to cancel').

components.note: 钅 (metal) — clocks and bells like 钟 were traditionally made of metal.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 钟.

example.english: What time is it now?
example.fact: 钟 originally meant 'bell'; because early clocks chimed the hour with a bell, it also became the word for 'clock,' as in 钟表 (zhōngbiǎo).

meanings: abbr. for Shijing 詩經|诗经[Shi1 jing1], the Book of Songs

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诗 names words arranged in verse, poetry.
寺 (sì) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading shī has diverged.

example.pinyin: Lǐ Bái xiě le hěn duō shī.
example.english: Li Bai wrote many poems.
example.fact: Li Bai is one of the most celebrated poets in Chinese history, from the Tang dynasty, and his poems are still memorized by schoolchildren today.

meanings: Tibet Autonomous Region (short name for 西藏自治區|西藏自治区[Xi1 zang4 Zi4 zhi4 qu1])

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 藏 relates to hiding something among vegetation.
臧 (zāng) gives a rhyme close to cáng, sharing a similar initial.

example.pinyin: Māo xǐhuan bǎ wánjù cáng qǐlai.
example.english: Cats like to hide their toys.
example.fact: 藏 means 'to hide, to store,' and when read with a different tone (Zàng) it refers to Tibet, as in 西藏 (Xīzàng) — the same character with two different readings.

meanings: to overtake; to catch up with

components.note: 走 (to walk, to run) — 赶 relates to pursuing or hurrying, both forms of movement.
干 (gān) gives a rhyme close to gǎn, with the tone shifted.

example.english: We need to hurry to the airport.
example.fact: 赶 combines with 紧 to form 赶紧 (gǎnjǐn, 'hurry up, quickly'), a very common word for urging speed.

meanings: theatrical work (play, opera, TV series etc)

components.note: 刂 (knife) contributes to the character's form, though its link to 剧's meaning 'drama' has faded over time.
居 (jū) gives a rhyme close to jù, with the tone shifted.

example.english: This TV drama is very famous.
example.fact: 剧 appears in 电视剧 (diànshìjù, 'TV drama') and 京剧 (Jīngjù, 'Peking Opera'), one of China's most famous traditional performance art forms.

etymologyHint: Flames 覀 over an altar 示, referring to a Chinese tradition of burning fake money as an offering

components.note: 覀 here depicts rising flames.
示 (altar) — burning paper offerings over an altar, a traditional practice, gave 票 its meaning of a paper note, later 'ticket, banknote.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le liǎng zhāng diànyǐng piào.
example.english: I bought two movie tickets.
example.fact: 票 refers to any small piece of valuable paper — tickets (电影票), banknotes (钞票), and ballots (选票) are all 票.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 损 relates to damage or loss caused by an action.
员 (yuán) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading sǔn has diverged.

example.pinyin: Dà fēng sǔnhuài le hěn duō fángzi.
example.english: The strong wind damaged many houses.
example.fact: 损 combines with 坏 to form 损坏 (sǔnhuài, 'to damage') and with 失 to form 损失 (sǔnshī, 'loss'), both common in news reports.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 忽 describes a mental state, a sudden shift in attention.
勿 (wù) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading hū has diverged.

example.english: He suddenly laughed.
example.fact: 忽 combines with 然 to form 忽然 (hūrán, 'suddenly'), one of the most common words in Mandarin for an abrupt change.

etymologyHint: A hand holding a large carpenter's square 工

components.note: 巨 depicts a hand gripping a large carpenter's square, a tool for measuring right angles — an image linked to great size, giving 巨 its meaning 'huge, giant.'

example.hanzi: 蓝鲸是世界上最巨大的动物。
example.pinyin: Lánjīng shì shìjiè shàng zuì jùdà de dòngwù.
example.english: The blue whale is the largest animal in the world.
example.fact: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived on Earth.

components.note: 火 (fire) — cannons like 炮 fire using explosive force.
包 (bāo) gives a rhyme close to pào, sharing a related initial.

example.english: Ancient cannons were very heavy.
example.fact: 炮, read as páo, also means 'to stir-fry quickly over high heat' — an unrelated cooking meaning sharing the same character.

etymologyHint: Older than 丨 the sun 日

components.note: 丨 is a simple vertical stroke, a marker element in this character's form.
日 (sun, day) — 旧 relates to the passage of many days, giving it the meaning 'old, former.'

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí liàng jiù qìchē.
example.english: This is an old car.
example.fact: 旧 is the opposite of 新 (xīn, 'new'), and the pair 新旧 (xīnjiù, 'old and new') is common when comparing things over time.

components.note: 立 (to stand) — 端 relates to standing upright, being straight and proper.
耑 (duān) gives the sound — an exact match with 端.

example.english: He stands very upright.
example.fact: 端 means 'end, extreme' or 'upright, proper,' and appears in 端午节 (Duānwǔ Jié, 'Dragon Boat Festival'), a major traditional Chinese holiday.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 探 describes reaching out with the hand to search for something.

example.english: Scientists are exploring space.
example.fact: Humans have sent spacecraft to explore every planet in our solar system, a major achievement of modern space exploration.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 湖 names a body of water, a lake.
胡 (hú) gives the sound — an exact match with 湖.

example.pinyin: Xīhú shì Zhōngguó yǒumíng de hú.
example.english: West Lake is a famous lake in China.
example.fact: West Lake, in Hangzhou, is one of China's most famous scenic spots and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

etymologyHint: A brush used to record stories

components.note: 录 traditionally depicted a hand-held tool used for carving or writing records — the image behind its meaning 'to record, to write down.'

example.english: Please record this meeting.
example.fact: 录 combines with 记 to form 记录 (jìlù, 'to record, a record') and with 音 to form 录音 (lùyīn, 'sound recording').

example.english: In autumn, tree leaves turn yellow.
example.fact: In autumn, many trees' leaves change color from green to yellow, orange, or red as chlorophyll in them breaks down.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 春 relates to spring's longer, sunnier days.

example.pinyin: Chūntiān lái le, huā dōu kāi le.
example.english: Spring has come, and the flowers have all bloomed.
example.fact: Spring is the season when many plants bloom and animals become active again after winter.

example.english: My hometown is in the south.
example.fact: 乡 combines with 家 to form 家乡 (jiāxiāng, 'hometown'), a word carrying strong emotional weight in Chinese culture around one's roots.

meanings: to be close to; to be attached

components.note: 阝 (a mound, a place) — 附 relates to being near or attached to a place.
付 (fù) gives the sound — an exact match with 附.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā fùjìn yǒu yí gè gōngyuán.
example.english: There is a park near my home.
example.fact: 附近 (fùjìn, 'nearby') is one of the most common words for describing location in daily Mandarin conversation.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吸 describes breathing in through the mouth.
及 (jí) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xī has diverged.

example.pinyin: Qǐng shēnshēn de xī yì kǒu qì.
example.english: Please take a deep breath.
example.fact: 吸 combines with 呼 to form 呼吸 (hūxī, 'to breathe'), and alone can mean 'to inhale' or 'to absorb,' as in 吸收 (xīshōu).

example.hanzi: 老师给予我们很多帮助。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī jǐyǔ wǒmen hěn duō bāngzhù.
example.english: The teacher gave us a lot of help.
example.fact: 予 is a formal, literary word for 'to give,' most often seen today in the compound 给予 (jǐyǔ, 'to grant, to give').

meanings: abbr. for 禮記|礼记[Li3 ji4], Classic of Rites

components.note: 礻 (spirit, altar) — 礼 relates to ceremony and rites performed before the spirits.
乚 reflects the character's phonetic root, though its exact link to the modern reading lǐ is unclear today.

example.english: Chinese people place great importance on politeness.
example.fact: 礼 relates to ceremony and propriety, appearing in 礼貌 (lǐmào, 'politeness') and 礼物 (lǐwù, 'gift') — both central to traditional etiquette.

meanings: Hong Kong (abbr. for 香港[Xiang1 gang3])

components.note: 氵 (water) — 港 names a harbor, a body of water.
巷 (xiàng) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading gǎng has diverged.

example.hanzi: 香港是一个国际化的城市。
example.pinyin: Xiānggǎng shì yí gè guójìhuà de chéngshì.
example.english: Hong Kong is an international city.
example.fact: Hong Kong is one of the world's busiest ports and a major global financial center.

etymologyHint: Rain drops falling from a cloud 帀

components.note: 雨 is a simplified picture of raindrops falling from a cloud.

example.english: It will rain tomorrow.
example.fact: Rain forms when water droplets in clouds become too heavy to stay suspended in the air and fall to the ground.

meanings: particle used to express surprise or mild emphasis
(Cant.) slurred form of the number ten
(particle equivalent to 啊 after a vowel, expressing surprise or doubt)

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呀, a spoken particle, comes from the mouth.
牙 (yá) gives the sound — an exact match with 呀.

example.english: Oh, you're here!
example.fact: 呀 is a sentence-final particle that softens a statement or adds surprise, common in casual spoken Mandarin.

components.note: 木 (wood) — boards and planks like 板 are traditionally made of wood.
反 (fǎn) gives a rhyme close to bǎn, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 黑板上写着今天的作业。
example.pinyin: Hēibǎn shàng xiězhe jīntiān de zuòyè.
example.english: Today's homework is written on the blackboard.
example.fact: 板 names flat, rigid objects generally — 黑板 (hēibǎn, 'blackboard'), 木板 (mùbǎn, 'wooden board'), and 铁板 (tiěbǎn, 'iron plate') all share this root meaning.

etymologyHint: A wide 广 couryard 廷; 廷 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 广 depicts a roofed building or shelter.
廷 depicts an open court or hall — together with the shelter above, giving 庭 its meaning 'courtyard, hall.'

example.hanzi: 他们在法庭上讨论这个案子。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài fǎtíng shàng tǎolùn zhège ànzi.
example.english: They are discussing the case in court.
example.fact: 庭 appears in 家庭 (jiātíng, 'family') and 法庭 (fǎtíng, 'courtroom') — from an open courtyard to the more abstract sense of a household or a court of law.

etymologyHint: Simplified form of 婦; a woman 女 with a broom 彐

components.note: 女 (woman) forms the left side of the character.
彐 depicts a broom — a woman holding a broom, a traditional image of housework, gave 妇 its meaning 'married woman, wife.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi jiātíng fùnǚ.
example.english: She is a housewife.
example.fact: 妇 combines with 女 to form 妇女 (fùnǚ, 'women' collectively), the term used in International Women's Day, 国际妇女节.

etymologyHint: Simplified form of 歸; a wife 帚 returning home; 追 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 彐 here depicts a broom, standing in for 帚 in the traditional form 歸 — the image of a wife returning home with her broom gave 归 its meaning 'to return.'

example.english: He finally returned to his hometown.
example.fact: 归 combines with 回 to form 回归 (huíguī, 'to return'), a word often used for the return of Hong Kong to Chinese sovereignty in 1997 (香港回归).

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睛 names the eyeball, part of the eye.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 睛.

example.english: Her eyes are very big.
example.fact: 睛 almost never stands alone — it always appears paired with 眼 in 眼睛 (yǎnjing, 'eye').

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饭 names cooked rice, a meal.
反 (fǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 饭.

example.english: Let's eat together.
example.fact: 吃饭 (chīfàn), literally 'eat rice,' is the general way to say 'eat a meal' in Mandarin, even when the meal has no rice at all.

components.note: 页 (head) — 额 names the forehead, part of the head.
客 (kè) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading é has diverged considerably.

example.english: His forehead is quite high.
example.fact: 额 also means 'a fixed amount, a quota,' as in 金额 (jīn'é, 'sum of money') — an extended, more abstract sense of the word.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 含 originally meant to hold something in the mouth.
今 (jīn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading hán has diverged.

example.pinyin: Zhè píng yǐnliào hán hěn duō táng.
example.english: This bottle of drink contains a lot of sugar.
example.fact: 含 extended from 'to hold in the mouth' to the broader meaning 'to contain,' as in 含糖 (hán táng, 'to contain sugar').

components.note: 页 (head) is the semantic root here, though the exact link to 顺's meaning 'to follow' isn't fully clear today.
川 (chuān) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading shùn has diverged.

example.english: I wish you all the best.
example.fact: 顺 combines with 利 to form 顺利 (shùnlì, 'smoothly, successfully'), one of the most common phrases in Chinese well-wishes.

components.note: 车 (cart) — 输 originally meant to transport goods by cart.
俞 (yú) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading shū has diverged.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen de qiúduì shū le bǐsài.
example.english: Our team lost the game.
example.fact: 输 means both 'to transport' (as in 运输, yùnshū) and 'to lose' a game or competition — two quite different senses sharing one character.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摇 describes shaking or waving something by hand.
䍃 (yáo) gives the sound — an exact match with 摇.

example.english: The wind shook the tree.
example.fact: 摇 combines with 动 to form 摇动 (yáodòng, 'to shake, to sway') and appears in 摇滚 (yáogǔn, 'rock and roll' music).

etymologyHint: A call 召 to arms 扌; 召 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — suggests a gesture, a beckoning motion.
召 depicts a call or summons — a hand gesture calling someone over gave 招 its meaning 'to beckon, to recruit.'

example.english: The company is recruiting new employees.
example.fact: 招 combines with 聘 to form 招聘 (zhāopìn, 'to recruit'), a word seen on job postings all over China.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婚 relates to marriage, historically centered on the wife.
昏 (hūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婚.

example.english: They plan to get married next year.
example.fact: 婚 combines with 结 to form 结婚 (jiéhūn, 'to get married'), one of the most common life-event words in Mandarin.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 脱 relates to taking something off the body.
兑 (duì) gives a sound close to tuō, sharing a related initial.

example.english: Please take off your shoes before entering.
example.fact: In many Chinese and other Asian households, it's customary to take off shoes (脱鞋) before entering someone's home.

components.note: 衤 (cloth) — 补 means to mend or patch clothing.
卜 (bǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 补.

example.pinyin: Tā zài bǔ yí jiàn jiù yīfu.
example.english: She is mending an old piece of clothing.
example.fact: 补 also means 'to make up for, to supplement,' as in 补课 (bǔkè, 'makeup class') or 补习 (bǔxí, 'tutoring').

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谓 relates to saying or calling something.
胃 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 谓.

example.english: This is what's called success.
example.fact: 谓 almost always appears in 所谓 (suǒwèi, 'so-called, what is called'), a common way to introduce a term or definition.

components.note: 目 (eye) — supervising, 督's meaning, involves watching closely.
叔 (shū) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading dū has diverged.

example.english: The teacher supervises students doing homework.
example.fact: 督 combines with 监 to form 监督 (jiāndū, 'to supervise, to oversee'), a common word in workplace and government contexts.

components.note: 龶 depicts a poisonous plant, tying 毒 to its meaning 'poison.'
母 (mǔ) gives a rhyme close to dú, with the initial shifted.

example.pinyin: Yǒuxiē mógu yǒu dú, bù néng chī.
example.english: Some mushrooms are poisonous and can't be eaten.
example.fact: Many wild mushroom species are poisonous, and some look very similar to edible ones, so foraging without expert knowledge can be dangerous.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 油 names an oily liquid.
由 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 油.

example.english: Mom uses oil to cook vegetables.
example.fact: 油 refers to any oily liquid — cooking oil (食用油), gasoline (汽油), and petroleum (石油) are all 油.

etymologyHint: To clear 了 an illness 疒; 了 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 疒 depicts a person lying sick in bed, the 'illness' radical.
了 here depicts a resolving action — clearing away an illness gave 疗 its meaning 'to treat, to cure.'

example.english: The doctor is treating the patient.
example.fact: 疗 almost always appears in 治疗 (zhìliáo, 'to treat, treatment') or 疗法 (liáofǎ, 'therapy method').

etymologyHint: A man 方 traveling with a pack 氏 on his back

components.note: 方 here depicts a flag or banner, marking a group on the move.
氏 depicts a person following behind — together, a group traveling together, giving 旅 its meaning 'trip, journey.'

example.english: Our whole family is traveling to Japan.
example.fact: 旅 combines with 游 to form 旅游 (lǚyóu, 'to travel, tourism'), one of the most common words for leisure travel.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泽 names a marsh or pool, a body of water.

example.pinyin: Zhǎozé lǐ yǒu hěn duō zhíwù.
example.english: There are many plants in the swamp.
example.fact: Wetlands and marshes are important habitats that support a huge variety of plant and animal life.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 材 originally named timber.
才 (cái) gives the sound — an exact match with 材.

example.hanzi: 这张桌子是用好木材做的。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhāng zhuōzi shì yòng hǎo mùcái zuò de.
example.english: This table is made of good wood.
example.fact: 材 broadened from 'timber' to 'material' in general (材料, cáiliào) and to 'talent' (人才, réncái, 'talented person').

meanings: to go out (of a fire etc)
etymologyHint: To cover 一 a flame 火

components.note: 一 (a horizontal line) depicts something laid over the fire below.
火 (fire) — covering a flame to smother it gave 灭 its meaning 'to extinguish, to go out.'

example.english: Please put out the fire.
example.fact: 灭 combines with 消 to form 消灭 (xiāomiè, 'to eliminate') and appears in 灭火器 (mièhuǒqì, 'fire extinguisher').

meanings: (bound form) to pursue; to chase; to drive away

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 逐 means to chase or pursue, involving movement.
豕 (shǐ) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading zhú has diverged.

example.pinyin: Lièrén zhújiàn kàojìn nà zhī lù.
example.english: The hunter gradually got closer to the deer.
example.fact: 逐 combines with 渐 to form 逐渐 (zhújiàn, 'gradually'), and alone means 'to chase, to pursue,' as in 追逐 (zhuīzhú).

example.hanzi: 莫扎特是有名的音乐家。
example.english: Mozart is a famous musician.
example.fact: Mozart was a renowned composer from Austria in the 18th century, still famous worldwide today.

meanings: writing brush; writing implement (pen, pencil etc) (CL:支[zhi1],枝[zhi1])
(bound form) style of writing; literary manner; technique of brushwork
etymologyHint: A bamboo rod ⺮ tipped with hair 毛

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) depicts the shaft of a writing brush.
毛 (hair) depicts the bristled tip of the brush — together giving 笔 its meaning 'writing brush, pen.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng yòng bǐ xiě nǐ de míngzi.
example.english: Please write your name with a pen.
example.fact: 笔 originally meant a traditional Chinese writing brush, and its meaning later extended to any writing tool — pens, pencils, even styluses.

etymologyHint: A man 人 in a coffin; see 亾

components.note: 亡 is traditionally read as a person enclosed within a coffin or hidden away — an early image behind its meaning 'to die, to be lost.'

example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng yǔyán yǐjīng xiāowáng le.
example.english: This language has already died out.
example.fact: Many languages around the world have gone extinct over history as their last speakers passed away, a process linguists call language death.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲜 originally described fresh fish or meat.
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 鲜.

example.english: This fruit is very fresh.
example.fact: 鲜 originally referred to fresh fish or meat, and later broadened to mean 'fresh' for anything, as in 新鲜 (xīnxiān).

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 词 names a word, a unit of speech.
司 (sī) gives the sound — an exact match with 词.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān xué le shí gè xīn cí.
example.english: I learned ten new words today.
example.fact: 词 is the word for 'word' itself in Mandarin, and also names a classical Chinese poetic form sung to music during the Song dynasty.

meanings: (literary) to dig with persistent effort (e.g. to gather wild vegetables)
(bound form) peerless (in wisdom, moral virtue, skill etc)
(bound form) peerless individual; paragon (sage, saint, emperor, master of a skill etc)
etymologyHint: Simplified form of 聖; a king 王 of listening 耳  and speaking口

components.note: 圣 is the simplified form of 聖, which combined an ear (耳, listening) and a mouth (口, speaking) above a standing figure — the image of someone who listens and speaks with special insight, giving 圣 its meaning 'holy, sacred.'

example.hanzi: 圣诞节是十二月二十五日。
example.pinyin: Shèngdàn Jié shì shí'èr yuè èrshíwǔ rì.
example.english: Christmas is on December 25th.
example.fact: Christmas is celebrated on December 25th in many countries around the world.

example.english: You can choose the color yourself.
example.fact: 择 almost always appears in 选择 (xuǎnzé, 'to choose, choice'), one of the most common decision-related words in Mandarin.

components.note: 彐 (a hand reaching out) — 寻 relates to searching, reaching for something.
寸 (cùn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xún has diverged.

example.hanzi: 我们在森林里寻找蘑菇。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài sēnlín lǐ xúnzhǎo mógu.
example.english: We are looking for mushrooms in the forest.
example.fact: 寻 combines with 找 to form 寻找 (xúnzhǎo, 'to search for'), pairing two near-synonyms for 'seek.'

meanings: "cliff" radical in Chinese characters (Kangxi radical 27), occurring in 原, 历, 压 etc

example.hanzi: 这家工厂生产汽车零件。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngchǎng shēngchǎn qìchē língjiàn.
example.english: This factory produces car parts.
example.fact: 厂 is also Kangxi radical 27, the 'cliff' radical, appearing in characters like 原 and 历, even though its own modern meaning is 'factory.'

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睡 relates to closing the eyes to sleep.
垂 (chuí) gives a sound partly close to shuì, sharing part of the rhyme.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān wǎnshang shí diǎn shuìjiào.
example.english: I go to sleep at ten every night.
example.fact: Doctors generally recommend that adults get around seven to nine hours of sleep each night for good health.

components.note: 十 (ten) — 博 relates to breadth, with ten symbolizing completeness.
尃 (fū) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading bó has diverged considerably.

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi bóxué de lǎoshī.
example.english: He is a very learned teacher.
example.fact: 博 means 'broad, extensive,' appearing in 博士 (bóshì, 'PhD, doctor') and 博物馆 (bówùguǎn, 'museum,' literally 'broad-things hall').

components.note: 力 (strength) — 勒 relates to tightening or restraining with force.
革 (gé) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading lēi has diverged considerably.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo shéngzi lēi de tài jǐn le.
example.english: This rope is tied too tight.
example.fact: 勒 as lēi describes something binding tightly, like a rope or strap; read with a different tone (lè), it also appears in transliterated place names such as 加勒比海 (Jiālèbǐ Hǎi, 'Caribbean Sea').

components.note: 火 (fire) — smoke, 烟's meaning, rises from fire.
因 (yīn) gives a rhyme close to yān, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 工厂的烟囱冒出很多烟。
example.pinyin: Gōngchǎng de yāncōng mào chū hěn duō yān.
example.english: Thick smoke billows from the factory's chimney.
example.fact: 烟 means both 'smoke' and 'cigarette' (as in 吸烟, xīyān, 'to smoke'), since cigarette smoke was the association that stuck.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 授 means to give or hand something over.
受 (shòu) gives the sound — an exact match with 授.

example.english: The professor is teaching a class to students.
example.fact: 授 appears in 教授 (jiàoshòu, 'professor') and 授课 (shòukè, 'to teach a class') — both centered on imparting knowledge.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诺 relates to a spoken promise or agreement.
若 (ruò) gives a rhyme close to nuò, sharing a related initial.

example.pinyin: Tā zūnshǒu le zìjǐ de chéngnuò.
example.english: He kept his promise.
example.fact: 诺 combines with 承 to form 承诺 (chéngnuò, 'promise, commitment'), a common word in both personal and business contexts.

etymologyHint: The logical order 仑 of human 亻 society; 仑 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伦 relates to human relationships and social order.
仑 depicts an orderly, logical arrangement — combined with 亻, giving 伦 its meaning 'human relationships, order.'

example.pinyin: Zhōu Jiélún shì yǒumíng de gēshǒu.
example.english: Jay Chou is a famous singer.
example.fact: Jay Chou (周杰伦) is one of the most influential Mandopop singers and songwriters of the past few decades.

etymologyHint: A mountain 山 cliff 厂; 干 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 山 (mountain) forms the top of the character.
厂 depicts a cliff or overhang — combined with 山 above, suggesting the steep edge of land meeting water, giving 岸 its meaning 'bank, shore.'

example.english: The boat is approaching the shore.
example.fact: 岸 names the edge of land next to water, as in 海岸 (hǎi'àn, 'coast') and 河岸 (hé'àn, 'riverbank').

meanings: (bound form) Austria (abbr. for 奧地利|奥地利[Ao4 di4 li4])
(bound form) Olympics (abbr. for 奧林匹克|奥林匹克[Ao4 lin2 pi3 ke4])
etymologyHint: A person 大 discovering a house 宀 full of rice 米

components.note: 宀 (roof) depicts a house.
米 (rice) — a house full of rice suggested something deep and abundant, hidden within.
大 (a person) — a person discovering hidden depths gave 奥 its meaning 'mysterious, profound.'

example.hanzi: 奥运会每四年举办一次。
example.pinyin: Àoyùnhuì měi sì nián jǔbàn yí cì.
example.english: The Olympics are held once every four years.
example.fact: The Olympic Games take place every four years and bring together athletes from countries around the world.

etymologyHint: Children learning how to read 口 and write 肀 in school 广

components.note: 广 depicts a roofed building, a school or hall.
肀 depicts a hand holding a writing brush.
口 (mouth) — children reading aloud and writing in school gave 唐 its early meaning, later borrowed as the name of the Tang dynasty.

example.hanzi: 唐朝是中国历史上重要的朝代。
example.pinyin: Tángcháo shì Zhōngguó lìshǐ shàng zhòngyào de cháodài.
example.english: The Tang dynasty was an important dynasty in Chinese history.
example.fact: The Tang dynasty (618–907 AD) is widely regarded as one of the golden ages of Chinese poetry, art, and culture.

components.note: 买 (to buy) — 卖 (to sell) is the flip side of buying, the other half of a transaction.
买 (mǎi) gives a sound very close to mài, differing only in tone.

example.english: This store sells fruit.
example.fact: 卖 and 买 (mǎi, 'to buy') look almost identical and are often confused by beginners — 卖 has an extra stroke on top.

meanings: abbr. for 俄羅斯|俄罗斯[E2 luo2 si1]

components.note: 我 (wǒ) reflects the character's phonetic root, though the sound has diverged over time from the modern reading é.

example.hanzi: 俄罗斯是世界上最大的国家。
example.pinyin: Éluósī shì shìjiè shàng zuì dà de guójiā.
example.english: Russia is the largest country in the world by area.
example.fact: Russia is the largest country in the world by land area, spanning across two continents.

etymologyHint: A sudden 乍 flame 火; 乍 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炸 relates to a sudden burst of fire, an explosion.
乍 depicts something happening abruptly — combined with fire, giving 炸 its meaning 'to explode, to deep-fry.'

example.english: Mom likes fried chicken.
example.fact: 炸 has two very different senses depending on context — 'to explode' (爆炸, bàozhà) and 'to deep-fry' (炸鸡, zhájī) — both involving intense heat.

meanings: to carry (i.e. publish in a newspaper etc)

components.note: 车 (cart) — 载 means to carry or transport by vehicle.
哉 (zāi) gives a rhyme close to zài, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 这辆卡车能载很多货物。
example.pinyin: Zhè liàng kǎchē néng zài hěn duō huòwù.
example.english: This truck can carry a lot of cargo.
example.fact: 载 also means 'year' in formal writing, as in 一年半载 (yì nián bàn zài, 'a year or so'), an unrelated but common secondary meaning.

meanings: old name of several rivers (in Henan, Shaanxi, Sichuan and Anhui)

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洛 names a river.
各 (gè) gives a sound close to luò, sharing a related rhyme.

example.hanzi: 洛阳曾经是中国的首都。
example.pinyin: Luòyáng céngjīng shì Zhōngguó de shǒudū.
example.english: Luoyang was once the capital of China.
example.fact: Luoyang, named for the Luo River, served as the capital of China during several ancient dynasties.

etymologyHint: Someone 亻 who can build 建 things; 建 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) — 健 describes a person's physical condition.
建 depicts building or constructing — a person strong enough to build things gave 健 its meaning 'strong, healthy.'

example.english: Exercise makes the body healthier.
example.fact: Regular physical exercise is widely recommended by doctors for maintaining good health, at any age.

meanings: large room for a specific purpose
relationship between cousins etc on the paternal side of a family

components.note: 土 (earth) — 堂 names a hall, a large room built on the ground.
尚 (shàng) gives a rhyme close to táng, with the initial shifted.

example.english: We eat in the cafeteria.
example.fact: 堂 combines with 食 to form 食堂 (shítáng, 'cafeteria, dining hall'), a common feature of Chinese schools and workplaces.

components.note: 立 (to stand) — 旁 relates to standing to the side of something.
方 (fāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 旁.

example.english: I sit next to him.
example.fact: 旁边 (pángbiān, 'beside, next to') is one of the most common location words used in everyday Mandarin conversation.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宫 names a palace, a grand building.
吕 (lǚ) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading gōng has diverged considerably.

example.english: The Forbidden City is in Beijing.
example.fact: The Forbidden City (故宫) in Beijing was the imperial palace for Chinese emperors for centuries and is now a major museum.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喝 describes an action of the mouth, drinking.
曷 (hé) gives the sound — an exact match with 喝.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē yì bēi shuǐ.
example.english: I want to drink a cup of water.
example.fact: 喝 is one of the first verbs beginners learn, always followed by a drink, as in 喝茶 (hē chá, 'drink tea') or 喝咖啡 (hē kāfēi, 'drink coffee').

meanings: (used in combination with 給|给[gei3] or 出[chu1] etc) to lend
to make use of; to avail oneself of

components.note: 亻 (person) — 借 describes an action between people, lending or borrowing.
昔 (xī) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading jiè has diverged considerably.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng jiè nǐ de shū.
example.english: I want to borrow your book.
example.fact: 借 can mean both 'to borrow' and 'to lend,' with the direction shown by context, as in pairing with 给 (借给, jiègěi, 'to lend to').

etymologyHint: A leader 尹 giving orders 口

components.note: 尹 depicts a hand holding a staff of authority, a leader.
口 (mouth) — a leader giving spoken orders gave 君 its meaning 'ruler, monarch.'

example.hanzi: 古代的君主有很大的权力。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài de jūnzhǔ yǒu hěn dà de quánlì.
example.english: Ancient monarchs had great power.
example.fact: 君 appears in 君主 (jūnzhǔ, 'monarch') and is also used respectfully to address someone, similar to an old-fashioned 'sir.'

components.note: 示 (altar) — 禁 relates to sacred restrictions observed near an altar.
林 (lín) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading jìn has diverged.

example.english: Smoking is forbidden here.
example.fact: 禁 combines with 止 to form 禁止 (jìnzhǐ, 'to forbid, prohibited'), a phrase seen on signs everywhere in China.

meanings: Yin (the negative principle of Yin and Yang)
etymologyHint: The place 阝 of the moon 月; compare 阳

components.note: 阝 (a mound, a place) — 阴 relates to the shaded side of a hill.
月 (moon) — the moon, associated with night and shade, gave 阴 its meaning 'shady, overcast'; compare 阳, which uses 日 (sun) for the opposite, sunny meaning.

example.english: It's overcast today.
example.fact: 阴 and 阳 (yáng) together form 阴阳 (yīnyáng), the classical Chinese concept of two complementary forces balancing the universe.

components.note: 囗 (an enclosure) — a garden like 园 is an enclosed area of land.
元 (yuán) gives the sound — an exact match with 园.

example.english: The children are playing in the park.
example.fact: 园 names an enclosed area of plants or recreation — 公园 (gōngyuán, 'park'), 花园 (huāyuán, 'garden'), and 动物园 (dòngwùyuán, 'zoo') all end with 园.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谋 relates to discussing and forming a plan.
某 (mǒu) gives the sound — an exact match with 谋.

example.hanzi: 他们在谋划一个新计划。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài móuhuà yí gè xīn jìhuà.
example.english: They are planning a new project.
example.fact: 谋 appears in 阴谋 (yīnmóu, 'conspiracy') and 谋划 (móuhuà, 'to plan'), often carrying a sense of careful, sometimes secretive, planning.

meanings: Song of the Southern Dynasties (420–479) 南朝宋[Nan2 chao2 Song4]
etymologyHint: A building 宀 made out of wood 木

components.note: 宀 (roof) depicts a building.
木 (wood) — a wooden building gave 宋 its original meaning, later used as a surname and dynasty name.

example.hanzi: 宋朝出现了很多有名的诗人。
example.pinyin: Sòngcháo chūxiàn le hěn duō yǒumíng de shīrén.
example.english: Many famous poets emerged during the Song dynasty.
example.fact: The Song dynasty (960–1279 AD) is remembered for major advances in technology, such as movable-type printing and the compass.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 避 means to avoid, moving away from something.
辟 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 避.

example.hanzi: 开车时要避开危险的路。
example.pinyin: Kāichē shí yào bìkāi wēixiǎn de lù.
example.english: When driving, you should avoid dangerous roads.
example.fact: 避 combines with 开 to form 避开 (bìkāi, 'to avoid, to dodge'), and with 免 to form 避免 (bìmiǎn, 'to avoid, to prevent').

etymologyHint: A hand 扌 with claws 爪; 爪 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抓 describes an action done by hand, grabbing.
爪 depicts claws or fingers gripping something, reinforcing 抓's meaning 'to grab, to seize.'

example.english: Cats like to catch mice.
example.fact: Cats are natural hunters, and chasing small prey like mice is an instinct even in well-fed house cats.

etymologyHint: Grass 艹 and trees 木 flourishing in a garden 冖

components.note: 艹 (grass) forms the top of the character.
木 (tree), sheltered beneath a covering, together depict plants flourishing, giving 荣 its meaning 'glory, prosperity.'

example.hanzi: 这个国家的经济很繁荣。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā de jīngjì hěn fánróng.
example.english: This country's economy is very prosperous.
example.fact: 荣 combines with 繁 to form 繁荣 (fánróng, 'prosperous, flourishing'), often used to describe a thriving economy or city.

etymologyHint: An older 古 woman 女; 古 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姑 names a female relative.
古 (old) — combined with woman, originally suggesting an older female relative, an aunt, giving 姑 its meaning.

example.english: My aunt lives in Shanghai.
example.fact: 姑姑 (gūgu) specifically means a father's sister, another example of how Mandarin kinship terms specify exactly which side of the family a relative is on.

etymologyHint: Simplified form of 孫; a chain 系 of descent 子

components.note: 子 (child) forms the left side of the character.
小, standing in for a connecting thread in the traditional form 孫, links generations together, giving 孙 its meaning 'grandchild, descendant.'

example.pinyin: Yéye hěn ài tā de sūnzi.
example.english: Grandpa loves his grandson very much.
example.fact: 孙 is also a common Chinese surname, shared by the historical statesman Sun Yat-sen (孙中山), a key founding figure of modern China.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 逃 means to escape or flee, involving movement.
兆 (zhào) gives a rhyme close to táo, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 那只鸟从笼子里逃走了。
example.pinyin: Nà zhī niǎo cóng lóngzi lǐ táo zǒu le.
example.english: That bird escaped from the cage.
example.fact: 逃 combines with 走 to form 逃走 (táozǒu, 'to run away') and with 跑 to form 逃跑 (táopǎo, 'to flee'), both common in stories and news.

example.english: I brush my teeth morning and night every day.
example.fact: Dentists generally recommend brushing your teeth at least twice a day to prevent cavities and gum disease.

etymologyHint: Lumber 木 bound by rope 口

components.note: 木 (wood) — 束 depicts a bundle of wood.
口 here depicts a rope or band wrapped around the wood, binding it together, giving 束 its meaning 'to bind, a bundle.'

example.pinyin: Tā shōu dào le yí shù huā.
example.english: She received a bouquet of flowers.
example.fact: 束 is the measure word for a bundle of thin things, like 一束花 ('a bouquet of flowers') or 一束光 ('a beam of light').

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跳 describes an action done with the feet, jumping.
兆 (zhào) gives a rhyme close to tiào, with the initial and tone shifted.

example.english: Kangaroos move by jumping.
example.fact: Kangaroos are famous for moving almost entirely by hopping on their powerful hind legs, rather than walking.

components.note: 页 (head) — 顶 names the top of the head, the crown.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 顶.

example.english: He is standing on the mountaintop.
example.fact: 顶 names the highest point of anything — 山顶 (shāndǐng, 'mountaintop') and 头顶 (tóudǐng, 'top of the head') both use it this way.
